x.name: Aaron Levie
x.bio: ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI

tweets.text:
The world is going to be using coding agents for far more than anyone would have thought before. 

We’ll be building tools in all new categories, building software for companies that couldn’t afford it before, using agents to protect systems from cyber risk, automating research in life sciences, processing insane amounts of data in complex workflows, upgrading legacy systems and infrastructures, and hundreds of other use cases.

In short, by lowering the cost of code, we are going to do so much more with it. This will result in software becoming more useful and the leverage of engineers going up dramatically, which coincidentally will mean we need more of them, not fewer.

The way to the reconcile capability level of AI vs. GDP impact is that the diffusion of AI will take much longer than people think. And it will also show up in ways that are hard to measure in GDP immediately. 

You could bring the world’s greatest superintelligence to many workflows, and still be bound by the laws of corporate physics: getting data prepared and put into a pipeline, process reengineering and change management, aligning on how the new workflow should function, and so on.

Even after you solve all that, you’re still bound by the speed of the real world: waiting for a customer to respond to a proposal, getting a permit for a project, a drug discovery pipeline taking years to eventually reach the consumer, and so on. Not to mention lots of positive daily AI use-cases are entirely net neutral to GDP, at least in the near term.

AI diffusion is going to be the theme of the next decade. The upside is that there’s a tremendous amount of opportunity in building the bridges between superintelligence and real-world workflows.

tweets.text: i love looking at the @every slack https://t.co/tQU2kjg1le

this is a very good and well designed report

however, two impt assumptions in it that significantly change the analysis once you start to play with it:

1. the report assumes that jobs can be decomposed into tasks
2. the report models human tasks created by automation always as a fraction of automated tasks. in other words, the underlying assumptions is automation always reduces human labor (or at best leaves it the same)

taken in reverse order:

does automation always reduce human work?
in my experience, the answer is no. automation often creates multiples more work for humans. 

i have a full argument here (https://t.co/Lb7SUCe2pO) for why this is structurally true. but i think any honest analysis of the economic impacts of AI has to take work creation seriously. 

can jobs be decomposed into tasks?
yes, that is a useful lens. but lists of tasks is a way of looking at jobs—one that makes the question of how much of a job is automatable actually tractable. therefore, it's useful.

but this is not the full picture, it's just jobs as exposed to our method of questioning. 

a good example: under this model, where do the new tasks come from? are they just from bosses that add a list to the task list for workers to complete? where do those tasks come from? unless you can model that well you are missing a key term in the analysis (see the first point above.)

another way of looking at this, borrowing from wittgenstein and heidegger, is that a job is a particular way of seeing and caring about the world. an editor notices things a nurse doesn’t, and vice versa. what you care about shapes what you notice, what seems worth doing, and what counts as doing it well. you can make some of that explicit as a task list. but as your tools and circumstances change, the same cares can generate entirely new tasks. that process is part of the job.

the above is completely missing from this analysis (understandably because it's, by definition, very hard to model!) 

but if you take it seriously, it shoudl substantially change your perspective automation and jobs

tweets.text:
AI people have talked about x-risk for years, so why did this blow up to 130M+ views?

Some people think it was a plant. Maybe.
But we can’t ignore 4 factors:

1) timing. This hits different after mythos and huggingface, and shortly before IPO

2) action. The resignation makes it feel more real, makes him seem like a whistleblower/defector vs another commentator

2) standing. He came from pre training not safety, and he’s worked at both of the labs he indicts

3) the human element. He doesn’t warn about abstract technology but about specific people (ie, these lab execs are gambling with our lives). Introduces a whiff of insider gossip and scandal

4) narrative. There’s a clear protagonist (us), antagonist (lab execs), stake (10% risk of wipeout), conflict (everyday people vs irresponsible execs), sacrifice (his career), a moral frame, and a choice ahead

Is he right? Hopefully not. Is he a pawn? We’ve seen no evidence yet.

But the factors above would make anything more viral

This “AI might kill us all” prediction has caused alarm around the world; it’s even in local news in India

One takeaway here is that messaging, like beauty, is in the eye of the beholder. In some circles, this post would’ve been praised for candor and intellectual honesty, with no hubbub at all

But in just the last couple years, the set of people paying attention to AI safety has changed (and massively expanded!)

Posts like this are now seen by very different people with very different reactions

I take on good faith that Evan intended to be honest, not to frighten people. That’s reasonable because until pretty recently, the people focused on this have been a small, niche group of AI researchers

But the topic has broken containment; posts like this are now globally relevant and reach users, regulators, members of the general public - many of whom are already quite sufficiently anxious
A major reason people don’t trust AI companies is that people who work at AI companies keep saying you can’t trust people who work at other AI companies

x.name: alphaXiv
x.bio: High fidelity research

tweets.text:
“Speed Limit for Information Acquisition in Stochastic Learning Dynamics”

SGD doesn’t just optimize parameters, it gradually encodes information about latent structure in the data.

This paper models SGD as a stochastic process and derives a Fisher-information speed limit that upper-bounds how fast model parameters can acquire information, separating contributions from deterministic gradient drift and minibatch noise.

In linear regression, the bound predicts which latent variables are learned first and when their information-acquisition rate peaks, giving a quantitative way to study the order and timescale of representation formation during training.

https://t.co/70t0ZLQABj

“Design Docs Are All You Need”

AI coding agents usually modify existing code, which easily accumulates technical debt and loses global context as codebases evolve.

So this paper suggest to treat natural-language design docs as the source of truth and code as disposable. A DAG of self-contained docs is rebuilt from scratch by coding sub-agents after every spec change.

Their SMART ML performance library regenerates in 1.5-3 hours for ~$100 and reproduces hand-audited reference models to round-off precision, suggesting design docs can become the durable artifact while code becomes a generated build product.

https://t.co/SWRu48flif

“Fractal basins trap latent reasoning”

Why do reasoning models sometimes spend dramatically longer on harder problems?

This paper shows that latent reasoning can exhibit transient chaos. Hard problems create fractal basins where tiny changes in the initial latent state send reasoning down wildly different trajectories and convergence times.

The key mechanism is that models get temporarily trapped near unstable saddle points corresponding to nearly-correct solutions, like dead ends in mazes or almost-valid Sudoku grids.

Whats even more interesting is that these fractal dynamics emerge during training precisely when models develop multi-step reasoning and learn to escape incorrect solutions.

This reframes overthinking as a dynamical consequence of solving hard problems rather than simply wasted computation.

https://t.co/JIzkGRq8qM
